blocks.text: How much pain does a person have to take on, just to escape another kind of pain?
Key progress

items.label: IP
items.value: China utility-model patent — application in progress

items.label: Consultants
items.value: Nursing staff at 2 care homes; Profs. Minki & Rudi at Shanghai NYU

blocks.text: Current focus
Small-batch production validation (Apr–Jun 2026).

This is a design project about end-of-life care. It runs through the last two years of my high-school design coursework, and is also the main reason I took a gap year after senior year before going to university.

In my second year of high school, my grandmother was injured by a heavy iron gate at our complex. She had a joint-replacement surgery; my family told me. I went back on the weekend to be with her in the care home — slept on a small board beside her bed. Four beds, four old women in the room, and a caregiver also sleeping on a board, but at the door. Why the door? In case one of them, half-conscious, tries to leave in the middle of the night — so they can be caught in time before they get lost or fall.

Grandma was bright the day I came; she even walked an extra round with me during her rehab. She fell asleep early. I sleep light, my mind kept turning, and at some point I heard mumbling and a dull thud-thud on the bed rail. I turned over and saw the woman in the next bed rocking back and forth, sitting up; and the one in the bed beyond hers swinging her hand against the rail. Couldn't sleep? Why couldn't she sleep? I could faintly see her hands were being restricted. In the daylight I saw what it was — two blue, ugly things on their hands, the main pad wide like a ping-pong paddle, the wrist part cinched narrow and tied to the bed rails.

The caregiver told me — these are restraint gloves. The woman on the left, called Xiaochun, kept trying to go home at night, running out, so the gloves went on, and they pinned her name onto her clothes. The woman on the right, Xiaocao, has been there the longest — she's paralysed below the waist, and an earlier care home didn't look after her well, so she came in with multiple bedsores; by now she's confused, can't really communicate. They can't sleep, must be some pain in body or mind. Could this all be otherwise? I decided to start there — that's where the research and the time-with-the-residents began.
Why restraint, and what it costs

Protective restraint is generally used when a patient can't safely control their own movement — to prevent falls, self-harm, accidental extubation, and other dangerous behaviour. It shows up in the disabled, the cognitively fluctuating, in emergencies and in long-term care.

columns.title: Without restraint, accidents still happen
items: falls
self-harm
unplanned extubation
other nursing adverse events

columns.title: With restraint, new harm emerges
items: agitation
psychological distress
compressed range of motion
poor fit on contracted hands
serious adverse events — finger necrosis, fatal asphyxiation

blocks.title: Death Due to Physical Restraint
blocks.text: A 2022 incident in China: an elderly person's hand got trapped by the «finger-separator ring» inside an opaque mesh glove, the fingers necrosed, and it was only discovered a week later. The protocol asks caregivers to «open and check the glove every 2 hours» — but in real workloads that's almost impossible to do consistently. A design can't put the most critical risk back on the user's discipline; it has to reduce blind spots structurally — for example, by making the mesh transparent. And the «finger separator», intended to keep fingers from injuring each other or scratching the face, doesn't actually stop self-harm. What stops self-harm is never tighter restraint.
Restraint and long-term bed rest
How common is restraint, and how does it sit with long-term bed rest? Both questions matter.
First-hand observation

The care home I visited practises a «minimum restraint» principle. Even so, 39% of residents wear restraint gloves; of those, 92% are also bedridden long-term. 53% of all residents are bedridden long-term, and 68% of that group wear restraint gloves. In the care environment I observed, restraint gloves aren't a niche tool — they're a common reality of care.

When I went back to the care home the next week, my grandma had been discharged. The new woman in the corner bed was a hearing-impaired old lady with soft, curving eyes; Xiaochun and Xiaocao were still in restraints. The caregivers worked efficiently; I helped feed Xiaocao her liquid food. My hands weren't practised, but if I was here as a volunteer, I'd do what I could do. I remembered how adults feed children — bite by bite, with encouragement. «One mouthful and your body gets stronger!» Xiaocao nodded firmly, murmuring «good, good, good». After the meal I dabbed her mouth, and thought, let me try talking to her.

«Next year I'll be 18, I can learn to drive» — I mimed it. Xiaocao's eyes went wide; she nodded, murmuring back. The conversation opened. She listened carefully, her hands struggling less. She'd repeat short words, but they could be understood. I heard her say «amazing, amazing», and «hurt, hurt, hurt». I pressed gently around her arm — «is it here?» — «yes, yes, yes». But every spot I pressed she said yes. Sometimes she tried to reach up and scratch her face; the blue glove edges scraped her. I folded a tissue and brushed her cheek with it. This time she said: «you're good, you're good, you're good».
I thought — she isn't confused at all.

The caregiver laughed and said — let her enjoy the company. Then told me: her family went abroad a long time ago, and recently sent her a box of mangoes — imported, apparently. «No one usually spends time with her like this.» I asked the caregiver to teach me how to tie the restraint glove on. «Two fingers' width, loose enough not to choke and tight enough she can't get out — see.» When she took the glove off, there wasn't even a red mark on the wrist; she's good at this. Xiaocao's hands had contracted, the joints behind them layered with old and new bruising from striking the rail. The glove cushions impact — but it can't cushion the obsession driving her to strike and swing her hands.
How much pain does a person have to take on, just to escape another kind of pain?

Xiaocao said «don't go» most often — and her hands started waving. I said I won't, I'm here, and she said «you're good». When their nap time came we had to stop talking. We laid the bed board out with the caregiver and stepped away. She murmured at the ceiling; the words I could pick out blurred into noise and her hand kept tapping. I stepped close and her eyes came alive again. I didn't dare give her my full company — if she got used to it and then called and I wasn't there, maybe forgetting me would be kinder.
Xiaochun

Xiaochun called me a thief the first time we met and told me to get out. The second time she pulled me close and warmly introduced — in dialect — the building outside the window that delivered her milk. Her family comes by often: a middle-aged couple, three or four times a week, bringing home-cooked food, helping her wash up, sitting with her. Originally they were caring for her at home, but Xiaochun kept trying to leave at night. They could stop her once, twice — not over a week or a month. So she came to the care home. They hate seeing the blue bag on her hand; once they couldn't help loosening it. That night, Xiaochun got loose, got out of bed, and by the time the caregiver noticed there was waste all over the floor. «Hm — we signed the consent saying we'd trust this place. Trust, trust, it's hard.» I don't quite remember if her family said that or the caregiver did.

Xiaochun could join the afternoon rehab activity. I went with her and watched her arguing with the numbers on the machine, determined to drag a stool onto the walking treadmill. She was in a wheelchair, then suddenly stood up to grab it; I jumped in to steady her. A while later I quietly moved the stool back down; she saw, frowned, and the stool was back on the treadmill. Sometimes she'd walk to the floor-to-ceiling window, curious, knocking on the glass, looking confused. The sun was good and Xiaochun was strong. Could there be a day when she forgets her legs are weak and just walks?
Back at school I started studying the restraint products already on the market.
The common «blue glove»
Meets the basic restraint function, but lacks on both user experience and caregiver usability.
«Humane-design» restraint glove
Introduces tactile-comfort pieces, but in doing so takes over the entire hand space; combined with rough mesh it backfires. Caregiver-side features are better updated, though.
Spatial / 360° restraint glove
360° protection, but the harder shell produces a knocking sound many elders can't tolerate, and the rigidity doesn't fit hand shape comfortably.
Non-restraint products
Synthesis

Some of these details — the ones you don't notice at first glance, but only see the value of once you've actually used the thing. One example: a transparent and sturdy mesh — both lets the caregiver check the hand at any moment, and lets the elderly person keep visual contact with their own hand, encouraging movement instead of letting it disappear into a black box.
No working features yet — concept only. Three structures.
1 · A glove body with soft pinch-pieces and inner space
2 · Air bladder for different arm-rest positions
3 · Electronic interaction button for loneliness relief
Feedback

items: Without any explanation, elders naturally start kneading the soft piece when they touch it. Some users find the base plate digs into their ulnar styloid.
Caregivers suggest: since there's already a bladder, make it a massage device instead — the «different rest positions» part isn't much needed.
Families like the button direction; they ask, but if a person is lucid enough to use the button, do they still need a restraint glove?

blocks.summary: V2 (2025 – 2026) · focus on the minimum-viable product

blocks.text: Focus on getting the glove body production-ready. Different sizes / materials of pinch-pieces, removable wrist cushioning, structural adjustments closer to real care needs.

items: For severely contracted hands, an ergonomic moulded shape is less useful than a simple adaptive foam ball.
For elders still wanting to move but with severe contracture, design slim adaptive rub-bars to put into the palm.
Wrist cushion is a nice piece, but not essential.
Long base plate, left/right hand cosmetic differentiation, and excess weight all add cost and burden.
Add a clinical-access window over the fingers.

blocks.text: Continue refining the glove body. Pitch approaching, so V1's massage and button features get rough basic prototypes.

items: New glove built on the feedback — resized, finger-access window, base-plate redesign, plus a new removable-base-plate opening.
Pinch balls and bars of different softness — foam balls (more sensory feedback, more stress-relief) and softer sponge.
Massage module — basic prototype, fits hand without air bladders.
Simple Bluetooth button module integrated with V1's ergonomic pinch block, can remote a computer.

blocks.text: Feedback

items: Glove body still needs micro-tuning: smaller body, narrower-longer wrist fabric. The tightest range still needs to be tighter. Fabric can be fluffier and thicker, cushion + protect, but never hard. Removability may not be that critical — over-fixing can actually pin down what should be free.

Pinch balls and bars also useful for elders not wearing restraint — one woman wouldn't let go of a pinch piece, so I gave it to her. The care home director stresses: material must be sweat-absorbing and easy to clean. Families say the pinch pieces are practical — when the body's uncomfortable, hands fidget; tactile distraction helps; and the pinch products on the market mostly don't work for contracted hands.
Massage is anticipated for future development.
Button is validated as useful: (1) for non-restrained elders who can't operate a phone precisely; (2) for the subset of restrained-but-still-button-capable elders.

blocks.text: What is the world of the elderly like? Today's physical and mental pain may be the most comfortable hour of the next year. The person who once raised others has become the person who needs care. Where does the meaning of the remaining time go? Even if design eases the pain, the emptiness of mind isn't something design can fill. And among the restrained elderly, too many are still clearly feeling everything.
So the reason I want to add a Bluetooth button on top of all this design is that — connected to a phone app it could mean:

items: Custom shortcut to call a caregiver or a family member.
Custom gesture inside an app — e.g. open the photo album, tap to advance to the next photo; or open a favourite TV show and tap to change the channel.
Cast to whichever device is in the room — a computer, a TV, a projector — no need to buy something new.

blocks.text: I sometimes think — the «information bubble» the internet gives young people is a kind of addictive ill design. But for an elderly person with empty time and loneliness, it could be a kind of «mental anaesthetic» — and, under restraint, a tiny piece of autonomy.

Autonomy matters so much, even just one small pinch piece you can squeeze. A pinch piece stuffed with foam doesn't even need complicated design. I've thought about why no one already makes a design a high-school student could come up with: maybe the need doesn't actually exist? But the families I met, the people around me, the stories of elders close to me — all tell me the need is there.

Early March, I met an older sister designing products for marginalised groups, and showed her this project. She kept rolling the sample in her hands, said her grandfather passed a while ago, and wore «the blue gloves» for the last year of his life. He'd loved watching TV. He didn't watch a single show that year. «This is really good, if there was a product like this,» she said, kneading the sample, «a lot of families would have another option.»

I've thought about going to university first, working a few years, coming back to push this as a more experienced designer. But of the families who already want to buy this design, two of the elders have already passed. Time doesn't wait. Especially when another possibility already exists.
I think I can keep doing this for a long, long time.
I. Core strategy

items: Take the «non-medical-device» path first to validate real purchase intent — test with about 50 pairs.
Don't rely on pitch outcomes. Whether or not there's funding, fund the first batch myself.
Goal isn't profit; it's market validation while not losing money.

blocks.text: II. Positioning

items.label: Restraint glove
items.text: Positioned as «nursing aid», not medical device. Function is preventing scratching and providing comfort — no medical claims.

items.label: Pinch / rub module
items.text: Independent soothing pad — non-toxic, kneadable. Not a medical device. Lower barrier; sold solo or as accessory.

blocks.text: III. First batch plan (~50 pairs + 100 modules)

items.label: Glove (basic)
items.value: 60 units / 30 pairs — uniform size, small-batch retail validation

items.label: Pinch modules
items.value: 100 units / 50 pairs — different specs; sellable solo or together

items.label: Gifts / samples
items.value: 12 gloves / 6 pairs; 18 modules / 9 pairs (Liang Yue, Lin Lan, DT, three nursing homes for trial)

items.label: Interview samples
items.value: 6 gloves / 3 pairs; 6 modules / 3 pairs (given to interviewees after)

items.label: Cost estimate
items.value: At most ¥10 000, covered out of my own pocket.

blocks.text: IV. Sales & validation path

items.label: Taobao store
items.text: Price per actual cost; pinch modules sold separately.

items.label: Xiaohongshu
items.text: Cut interview footage and product stories; reach non-medical-context users first.

items.label: Early-buyer policy
items.text: First batch + gift recipients + interviewees + acknowledgment list become «permanent VIPs» with future discounts.

items.label: Pre-order
items.text: If first batch sells out, second is «batch when enough orders are collected» — no discount, just volume.

blocks.text: V. Interviews & feedback (final validation)

items.label: Stage 1 · before production
items.text: Take the latest prototype back to the care home; have residents try it; collect notes from caregivers and family. Goal: lock the drawing for production. An unexpected upside — one non-medical-context care home has ordered samples (3 gloves + 6 modules) for trial.

items.label: Stage 2 · after production
items.text: Use sample units for user feedback; continue interviewing caregivers and families; produce footage; gift the samples to participants as thanks.

columns.title: Good interview candidates
items: relatively lucid, can express feelings
calm-ish when wearing the glove
family present and open to talking
some clear current frustration with the glove

columns.title: Not the first interview group
items: severe agitation, unable to communicate
extreme rejection of any restraint
family absent or indifferent
bad past experience + family still very angry

blocks.text: VI. Risk management

items.label: Safety
items.text: Bio-compatible fabric, non-toxic filling, keep testing reports.

items.label: Labels
items.text: Clearly marked «nursing aid, not medical device», «use under supervision».

items.label: Legal line
items.text: No medical claims, no promise to treat.

items.label: Records
items.text: Sales through Taobao for traceable records.

blocks.text: VII. Long-term direction

items: If the home market responds well, scale up; add materials and shapes for the pinch modules into a «care-piece» line.
If care homes start buying, consider starting the medical-device filing and a «medical-grade» glove.
If response is flat, analyse and decide direction.

blocks.text: VIII. Support I'm looking for

items.label: Direction
items.value: Help me sharpen judgments I've already partly made.

items.label: Medical network
items.value: CRO, medical-device factories, filing consultants, care-home procurement, industry experts.

items.label: Endorsement
items.value: Stand with me — let the outside know this is a serious project.

blocks.text: But whether the support arrives or not, I'll fund the first 50 pairs myself and let the market answer first.
